heading: Key Antiseizure Selection Tips
text: Drugs rarely, if ever, used in pediatrics: carbamazepine (Tegretol), phenytoin (Dilantin).

heading: Drug rash risk
text: Avoid if prior serious rash such as SJS/TEN, DRESS.Higher‑risk: phenytoin (DPH), carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, zonisamide, felbamate.Consider instead: levetiracetam, valproate, benzodiazepines, brivaracetam, lacosamide.

heading: Sulfonamide (“sulfa”) issues
text: Contain sulfa moiety: topiramate, zonisamide, acetazolamide.In true severe sulfonamide allergy, most avoid these and favor levetiracetam, valproate, benzodiazepines, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine (if no serious rash history), lamotrigine with counseling, etc.

heading: Renal failure
text: Dose‑adjust / avoid accumulation.Need adjustment or extended interval: gabapentin, levetiracetam, zonisamide, topiramate.More hepatic/less renal clearance (often preferred in advanced CKD, with their own caveats): valproate, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide, clobazam.

heading: Hepatic dysfunction
text: Prefer: levetiracetam, lacosamide.Avoid or use great caution: valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, chronic benzodiazepines.

heading: Weight/metabolic concerns
text: Better: lamotrigine, levetiracetam; topiramate/zonisamide can cause weight loss but have cognitive/renal stone risks.Less ideal: valproate, carbamazepine, pregabalin.

heading: Kidney stones/metabolic acidosis
text: Avoid or monitor closely: topiramate, zonisamide, acetazolamide.Better: lamotrigine, levetiracetam, valproate.

heading: Psychiatric comorbidity
text: Mood‑friendly: lamotrigine, valproate (bipolar spectrum), clobazam.Potentially mood‑worsening: levetiracetam, brivaracetam, topiramate, phenobarbital.

heading: Women of childbearing potential
text: Prefer: lamotrigine, levetiracetam.Avoid if possible: valproate (especially generalized epilepsies), topiramate, phenytoin, phenobarbital.

heading: Generalized epilepsies
text: Use: valproate (if feasible), levetiracetam, lamotrigine, ethosuximide (absence), clobazam, topiramate/zonisamide.Avoid: carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, tiagabine.

heading: Focal epilepsies
text: Use: carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, lacosamide, cenobamate (older patients).Avoid: ethosuximide (absence‑only), vigabatrin unless specific indication.

heading: Cognitive concerns
text: Better: lamotrigine, levetiracetam, brivaracetam.Worse: topiramate, phenobarbital, chronic benzodiazepines, high‑dose zonisamide.

heading: Polypharmacy / interaction‑heavy patients
text: Preferred: levetiracetam, lacosamide, brivaracetam, gabapentin/pregabalin.Caution: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone (inducers), valproate (inhibitor).

heading: Acute Symptomatic Neonatal Seizures
text: Definition: Acute symptomatic (acute provoked) neonatal seizures are electrographic seizures that occur in close temporal association with an acute brain insult or systemic disturbance such as hypoxic‑ischemic encephalopathy, stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, infection, or significant metabolic derangement, in an infant without prior epilepsy. In current neonatal ILAE frameworks, seizures are defined electrographically: sudden, repetitive, evolving, and stereotyped EEG discharges with clear onset, evolution, and offset; clinical signs may be absent or subtle.

heading: Treatment
text: First line: phenobarbital (ILAE 2023), unless a channelopathy is suspected — then a sodium channel blocker.6 Second line: phenytoin, levetiracetam, midazolam, or lidocaine. Levetiracetam is preferred second line in cardiac disease.6 As single agents, phenobarbital achieved 43% and phenytoin 45% seizure control; combined, 57–62%.7 For 24-hour seizure freedom, phenobarbital 80% vs levetiracetam 28%.8

heading: Monitoring through rewarming
text: Continue EEG through rewarming, and beyond it if seizures are detected.9 More infants seized during rewarming than in the preceding 12-hour epoch: 27% vs 14% (72-h cooling) and 21% vs 10% (120-h cooling).9 Death or moderate-to-severe disability at 2 years was higher in those with rewarming seizures: RR 1.7 (1.25–2.37).9

text: Discontinue antiseizure medication before discharge once acute provoked seizures have resolved, regardless of MRI or EEG findings.10 No difference in outcome at 24 months.10 No difference out to school age — adjusted HR 0.93 (0.48–1.80) for epilepsy at 1–8 years.11

text: Acceptable forms: Tablets, capsules, IM, IV, rectal, nasal drops, sprays, nebulizers. Avoid: Chewables, oral suspensions/liquids/elixirs (use only if no substitute). Acceptable fever/pain meds: Brand name Tylenol 325 mg tabs/caps, 500 mg caps; Feverall rectal suppositories (80, 120, 325 mg); Children’s Junior Motrin 100 mg caps; Advil 200 mg caps, 100 mg/5 mL (use sparingly — contains some carbs). heading: Vagus Nerve Stimulator (VNS)
text: VNS is not a cure. It is used to help control or lessen the severity of seizures. VNS is discussed prior to implantation at the epilepsy surgery conference to determine eligibility.

heading: Basics for Families
text: The generator is implanted under the skin of the chest; electrodes wrap around the left vagus nerve in the neck. A stimulus is sent to the vagus nerve at programmed intervals to attempt to prevent seizures. Newer devices (Model 106 and Sentiva) monitor heart rate and deliver a slightly higher current for rapid heart-rate changes that may be associated with seizures. VNS is activated just after implantation and ramped up via clinic visits and automatic protocols every 1–2 weeks. Battery lasts 6–10 years; generator must be surgically replaced. The lead on the vagus nerve is generally not removed

heading: Using the Magnet
text: Swipe the magnet over the generator for a count of 3 seconds. Once the magnet is removed, the generator provides a higher-amplitude pulse for ~60 seconds to try to abort the seizure or shorten the postictal period. The magnet can never be used too much or damage the device. The VNS can only be activated every 60 seconds regardless of how many times you swipe.

heading: Side Effects and Temporary Shut-Off
text: Side effects: Local discomfort, throat pain, cough, changes in voice pitch/volume, reflux. These can usually be modulated by adjusting VNS settings. OSA can be an adverse effect — increased daytime sleepiness or worsening snoring should be evaluated with PSG. To temporarily turn off: Place the magnet over the generator and tape it in place with heavy tape. As long as the magnet is over the generator, no current is delivered. Remove the magnet to resume normal stimulation.

heading: Imaging and Surgery Considerations
text: The VNS lead is ferromagnetic and may heat up in a strong magnetic field. MRI should not be performed of the chest and upper spine. Before MRI: set output current to zero (can be done by EEG techs/APPs in EMU for inpatients or clinic RNs for outpatients). Restore settings after scan. Electrocautery during surgery can affect the device. Interrogate before and after surgery to ensure proper function. text: Infantile spasms (IS) is an epilepsy of early infancy, affecting 3-4.5/10,000 live births, with typical onset 1-15 months (peak 4-9 months), M>F. heading: Prognosis
text: Resolution of spasms is associated with better developmental outcomes. The primary driving factor is treatment with a standard first-line therapy (ACTH, prednisolone, or vigabatrin).In children with known etiology, prognosis is related to etiology. heading: Shuddering Attacks
text: Age: usually 4–12 months. Phenomenology: sudden brief "shiver" or tremor of head/shoulders/trunk, often with facial grimace or arm stiffening; parents describe "like ice‑cold water poured down the neck." Duration: 1–2 seconds; can recur many times daily. Awareness: intact; child continues activity; no postictal state. Triggers: excitement, feeding, frustration, or spontaneous. Course: benign; typically improve with age. Management: reassurance; no routine EEG or imaging when history and exam are typical.

heading: Breath‑Holding Spells (BHS)

heading: Paroxysmal Kinesigenic Dyskinesia (PKD)
text: Age: typically school‑age through adolescence. Phenomenology: brief attacks (seconds to <1 minute) of dystonia, chorea, or mixed dyskinesia (often unilateral or asymmetric); described as "twisting," "jerking," or "locking up." Trigger: sudden voluntary movement or start (standing up quickly, taking first step, running, sudden direction change); often many attacks per day. Awareness: preserved; no postictal state. Between attacks: normal neurologic and developmental exam. Course: often familial; commonly associated with PRRT2 variants; excellent response to low‑dose carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine.

heading: Primary Motor Stereotypies vs Tics
text: Stereotypies Onset: infancy/early childhood (<3 years). Movements: rhythmic, patterned, prolonged (e.g., hand flapping, rocking). Triggers: excitement, engrossment; often when sitting or standing still. Awareness: intact; distraction can interrupt behavior. Course: long‑standing but non‑progressive. Tics Onset: usually >4–5 years. Movements: brief, non‑rhythmic, can migrate (eye blinks, throat clears, shoulder shrugs, etc.). Premonitory urge and relief after tic; suppression possible but uncomfortable. Course: waxing and waning over weeks–months.

heading: Sandifer Syndrome
text: Age: infancy/early childhood, often 2–18 months. Phenomenology: episodic, often dramatic arching and dystonic posturing of neck and trunk (opisthotonus, torticollis‑like), commonly around feeds. Association: gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and/or hiatal hernia; may have poor weight gain, irritability, or feeding aversion. Features suggesting Sandifer rather than seizure: Temporal relationship to feeding or supine positioning after feeds. Child usually alert and interactive between spells. Normal EEG. Management: reflux measures (thickened feeds, positioning, acid suppression when approp

heading: Benign Paroxysmal Vertigo of Childhood (BPVC)
text: Age: typically 2–6 years. Phenomenology: sudden episodes of vertigo/unsteadiness; child may grab caregiver, appear frightened, or fall; may have nystagmus, pallor, vomiting. Duration: minutes, then complete recovery. Association: strong personal/family history of migraine; often evolves into migraine later. Work‑up: normal neurologic exam between attacks; if atypical or persistent ataxia, perform MRI ± vestibular evaluation. Management: reassurance; treat as migraine variant if frequent (lifestyle, prophylaxis).

heading: Benign Paroxysmal Torticollis of Infancy
text: Age: onset usually 3–8 months, resolving by 3–5 years. Phenomenology: recurrent episodes of head tilt (often alternating sides) with pallor, irritability, vomiting, or ataxia. Duration: hours to days; normal baseline between episodes. Association: migraine spectrum; many later develop migraine. Work‑up: neurologic and ocular exam; imaging if baseline torticollis persists, there are focal deficits, or course is atypical. Management: reassurance; treat associated conditions (reflux, migraine triggers); PT if persistent neck tightness.

heading: Spasmus Nutans
text: Age: typically 4–18 months. Triad: Fine, high‑frequency (often asymmetric) nystagmus. Head nodding. Intermittent torticollis. Course: generally improves and resolves by age 3–4 years. Critical consideration: optic pathway or other intracranial lesions can mimic this presentation. Work‑up: detailed ophthalmologic exam; MRI brain and orbits with contrast if atypical age, visual symptoms, optic disc abnormalities, or persistent/progressive signs. Management: if imaging and ophthalmology are normal, reassure and monitor.

text: Small-molecule (intoxication/energy) disorders involve the accumulation of toxic small metabolites or failure of energy production. Because these metabolites are water-soluble and can be cleared — by dialysis, dietary manipulation, cofactors, or specific medications — many are highly treatable. This is the group you cannot miss. Large-molecule (organelle) disorders involve failure to process complex molecules within organelles (lysosomes, peroxisomes, Golgi). Damage accumulates structurally over time. heading: A Critical Nuance: Intoxication vs. Energy Failure
text: Within the small-molecule category, intoxication-type disorders (e.g., organic acidemias, UCDs, MSUD) and energy-failure disorders (e.g., FAODs, mitochondrial RC defects, GLUT1) are distinct. This matters clinically: organic acidemias cause toxicity from accumulating organic acids and often produce ketosis and metabolic acidosis; FAODs primarily cause energy failure during fasting and produce hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Mitochondrial disorders can present with either pattern or both. Recognizing the sub-type guides initial empirical management.

heading: Why Some IEMs Cause Episodic Disease and Others Cause Steady Decline
text: This depends on whether the pathological mechanism is acute metabolite accumulation (reversible if treated) vs. structural or irreversible cellular damage over time. In UCD or MSUD, ammonia or leucine rises during metabolic stress, causing encephalopathy — but the neuron itself can recover if the crisis resolves. In contrast, lysosomal storage with progressive lipid or substrate deposition is structural; neurons die. Many disorders are intermediate: basal ganglia injury in organic acidemias (irreversible stroke-like damage) can occur against a backdrop of episodic presentation.

Exam: distinctive features (dysmorphism, neurocutaneous signs), head size, organomegaly, movement disorder. MRI brain when focal deficits, abnormal head growth, refractory epilepsy, or concerning exam.

heading: Step 2 – Broad Genetic Testing
text: If the child meets criteria for global developmental delay (≥2 domains, moderate/severe) with any combination of ID, ASD, epilepsy, abnormal exam, or regression/evolving picture, or is not responding to standard treatment: Order trio WES/WGS as the primary test. Add targeted or syndrome‑specific panels only when clearly indicated.

heading: Step 3 – Additional Studies and Follow‑up
text: Chromosomal microarray (if not already done). Fragile X testing (especially males or suggestive family history). Metabolic testing that may have been missed, guided by phenotype. Consider EEG to evaluate for ESES or other epileptic encephalopathy patterns. Consider repeat MRI if concern for evolving leukodystrophy or basal‑ganglia changes. Refer to a Neurogenetics clinic when expedited, comprehensive evaluation or VUS resolution is needed.

text: Positive – pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant explaining the phenotype; guides management and family testing. Negative – no causative variant found; a genetic cause may still exist. Variant of uncertain significance (VUS) – uncertain; should not usually change management. Most reclassified VUS move downward toward benign/likely benign rather than toward pathogenic.

heading: GINA – Key Points for Families (U.S.)
text: GINA limits how health insurers and most employers can use genetic information. Health insurers cannot use genetic test results to set eligibility or premiums or require testing. Employers with ≥15 employees cannot use genetic information in hiring, firing, or promotion decisions. GINA does not cover life, disability, or long‑term‑care insurance, and does not apply to very small employers; families should understand these limits when deciding about testing.

heading: CN III Palsy — Surgical vs Medical
text: "Surgical" (pupil-involving): Mydriasis + ptosis + limited adduction/elevation/depression → concern for posterior communicating artery (PComm) aneurysm compression. Urgent CTA/MRA. "Medical" (pupil-sparing): Ptosis + eye movement limitation but normal pupil → microvascular (diabetes, hypertension). More common in adults; rare in children. In children: Pupil-sparing distinction is less reliable. Any CN III palsy in a child warrants imaging.

heading: Leukodystrophy Pattern Recognition
text: Leukodystrophies are genetically determined disorders of white matter — distinguished from acquired white matter disease by their symmetric, progressive, and anatomically patterned involvement. The single most useful first step is to identify the predominant WM pattern, which narrows the differential substantially before genetic testing is sent. The key distinction is between demyelination (myelin actively destroyed — typically progressive with MRI change) and hypomyelination (myelin never formed normally — T2-bright WM that does not progress on serial imaging). heading: Malformations of Cortical Development (MCD)
text: MCDs arise from disruption of the three sequential stages of cortical formation: proliferation (germinal zone, weeks 7–16), migration (radial/tangential, weeks 12–24), and organization/postmigration (synaptogenesis, weeks 24–postnatal). The earlier the disruption, the more severe and widespread the malformation. This mechanistic framework is worth knowing because it maps onto the imaging phenotype: migration defects produce heterotopia and lissencephaly; organization defects produce PMG and FCD. heading: Neonatal Brain Injury Patterns
text: Neonatal brain injury patterns reflect the interaction between the type and duration of the insult and the regional metabolic vulnerability at the gestational age of injury. Term and preterm brains are injured differently — because their most metabolically active and most vulnerable regions differ. Understanding this mapping between insult type, gestational age, and imaging pattern is the conceptual foundation for interpreting neonatal MRI. text: Radiation dose is measured by millisievers (mSv). Naturally occurring “background” radiation exposure is estimated to be 3 mSv per year.
